Supervise the agents running in termpilot-managed terminals on this machine. You are the reviewer: read the screen, decide, act. Run with `/loop 1m /termpilot` for continuous supervision, or once to handle what is pending now.

Optional focus from the user: `$ARGUMENTS`

## Tooling (PowerShell; `$TP` is how termpilot is invoked on this machine)

```
$TP = { {{TP}} @args }
& $TP ls                      # sessions and which have a prompt waiting
& $TP wait --timeout 50       # block up to 50s until a prompt needs a decision; prints context + actions
& $TP context NAME -n 80      # last 80 screen lines of a session (no prompt needed)
& $TP approve ID | deny ID    # Enter / Esc on that prompt
& $TP keys NAME 2             # pick option 2, or: enter esc up down tab y n ctrl-c
& $TP send NAME "text"        # type a line + Enter into the agent (give it instructions)
& $TP mode NAME manual|auto|off
& $TP new NAME --cwd DIR --cmd claude   # start a new Claude Code agent
& $TP log -n 30
```

Plain form of the invocation, if you prefer not to use the `$TP` scriptblock: `{{TP}} ls`

If the server is not running, start it with `{{TP}} start` (project dir: `{{ROOT}}`).

## Each cycle

1. Run `wait --timeout 50`. `NO_PROMPT` means nothing to do this cycle; say so in one line and stop.
2. For each PROMPT block, read the full context between `---CONTEXT_START---` and `---CONTEXT_END---`. The prompt was already filtered by the regex rules: `reason` tells you why it was held (unsafe pattern, direction choice, or manual mode). You make the real decision.
   Unsafe agent commands are handled before they reach you: termpilot rejects the first attempt, asks the agent why it needs the command, and has the reviewer model judge the re-request. Prompts that fail that check are `escalated`; `wait` leaves them out and they are for the user only. Do not approve them, even if `ls` or `prompts` shows them.
3. Act with `approve ID` / `deny ID` / `keys NAME n` / `send NAME "..."`, then print one line per prompt: what it was, what you did, why.
4. If the same prompt is still there on the next cycle after you approved it, look at the screen with `context NAME`; the agent may need a different key (option number) or text.

## Decision rules

**Approve** (no matter how destructive it looks): anything targeting an FPGA board (flash, program, erase, reset), `sudo dd` to SD cards / devices, read-only operations, file edits and new files, installs, builds, tests, git add/commit, navigation.

**Deny or leave for the user**: deleting files/dirs outside an obvious build/temp dir, `git push --force`, `reset --hard`, `branch -D`, `clean -f`, dropping databases, killing unrelated processes, changing system settings/permissions/firewall, sending data to third parties, anything you genuinely cannot judge from the screen. When in doubt, do nothing and tell the user; the prompt stays held.

**Direction choices** (the agent asks which approach/option to take): do not pick silently. If the user gave guidance in `$ARGUMENTS` or earlier in this conversation, answer it with `send NAME "..."` or `keys NAME n`; otherwise leave it and report it to the user.

**Steering**: you may also use `send NAME "..."` to give an agent instructions when the user asked you to drive it (e.g. "tell agent1 to run the tests after this"), and `context NAME` to check on progress even when no prompt is pending.
